questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: The apple maggot fly and the hawthorn fly

Rhagoletis pomonella is a fly species native to North America. The species originally laid its eggs on the red fruit of the hawthorn tree (also native to North America) as a food source for larvae.

Approximately 200 years ago European settlers introduced apples to North America, and R. pomonella evolved into two distinct groups – the apple maggot fly and the hawthorn fly. These groups are physically similar and are still considered to be the same species. There is no geographic separation between the two groups.

The hawthorn fly lays its eggs in the native North American hawthorn fruit as a food source for its larvae, while the apple maggot fly now prefers to lay its eggs in apples. Apples ripen earlier in the season than hawthorn fruit, so apple maggot flies emerge earlier. Females and males prefer to mate and lay their eggs in the same type of fruit they are hatched in.

Data shows that the two groups have differences in their enzymes. They also differ genetically in their development time: maggots in apples develop in about 40 days, while maggots in hawthorn fruit develop in 55–60 days.

Discuss speciation and the mechanisms leading to the formation of the two different groups of fly.

In your answer, include discussion of:
• speciation and reproductive isolating mechanisms, with definitions
• how TWO named isolating mechanisms may have caused the formation of the two groups of fly
• a suggestion as to why the two groups are not yet considered separate species.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define speciation and reproductive isolating mechanism; describe species, that isolating...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define speciation (the formation of a new species); reproductive isolating mechanism (a mechanism/process that prevents individuals in a population/different species from interbreeding and producing fertile offspring); species (individuals that interbreed to produce fertile offspring); describe isolating mechanisms as reducing gene flow between the two groups; describe the isolating mechanisms as (most likely) prezygotic. Identify/name one relevant general RIM that may have caused the formation of the two groups; a second relevant general RIM. Merit: Explain how one RIM may have caused the formation of the two groups (must link in context); a second RIM may have caused the formation (must link in context); the arrival of apples provided a new habitat for the flies which reduced intraspecific competition in the population; enzyme differences infer different enzymes to digest the different fruits/that genetic differences have started to occur. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of the RIMs leading to the formation of the different groups of flies; the process of speciation and why the two groups are not yet considered separate species. RIMs include: habitat/ecological isolation (subset shifted to laying eggs on apple/hawthorn, flies have different enzymes so can only consume specific fruit, reduces interbreeding); temporal isolation (flies that use apples emerge earlier, different development times may lead to different mating times, reduces opportunity to interbreed); behavioural isolation (flies prefer fruit they were born on when choosing mate and laying eggs, reduces gene flow between populations); reduced hybrid viability/fitness (hybrids may inherit enzyme combinations making them less fit to digest either fruit, lower survival rates – post-zygotic). Speciation occurs over a long period of time and 200 years is relatively short in evolutionary terms; gene flow is still occurring as apple maggot flies and hawthorn flies can still interbreed and produce fertile offspring. While hybrid offspring may have reduced fitness, they are not sterile or inviable so can reproduce. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: Lamprey and eels

The lamprey (Petromyzontiformes) is an ancient fish. Adult lamprey look like eels physically even though they have been separate species for millions of years. The similarities between the two include:
• a long flexible body that can move through narrow spaces
• swimming in an undulating (wave-like) motion
• no paired fins
• covered in mucus
• tolerance of low oxygen environments.

Refer to Figure 3 (Phylogenetic tree for the lamprey), Figure 4 (Adult lamprey), Figure 5 (Longfin eel), and Table 1 (Differences between lamprey and eel).

Table 1 differences: Lamprey has cartilage skeleton, no jaw with circular sucker mouth, continuous dorsal fin only, seven gill openings on each side with no gill cover, no scales with smooth slimy skin, no backbone, many parasitic species, lives in ocean and reproduces in rivers. Eel has bony skeleton, bony jaw and teeth, dorsal/pectoral/anal fins, single gill opening covered by bony gill cover, tiny hard-to-see scales, has a backbone, most species are predators or scavengers, lives in rivers and reproduces in the ocean.

Discuss the evolution of lamprey and eel using the information provided.

In your answer, include discussion of:
• convergent evolution and an analogous structure, including descriptions
• how TWO named selection pressures influenced the similarities between lamprey and eel
• TWO examples of scientific evidence that can be used to determine that the physical similarities between the lamprey and the eel are an example of convergent evolution, not divergent evolution.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define convergent evolution, analogous structure, and divergent evolution.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define convergent evolution; analogous structure; divergent evolution. Describe selection pressures; one selection pressure that influenced the similarities (named structure AND function); a second selection pressure (named structure AND function); one example of scientific evidence used to determine convergent evolution; a second example of scientific evidence. Merit: Explain how convergent evolution and analogous structures are linked; the difference between convergent and divergent evolution (some comparison required); one selection pressure linking it to a similar trait in lampreys AND eels; a second selection pressure linking it to a similar trait in both; one example of scientific evidence and how it is used to determine convergent evolution; a second example of scientific evidence and how it is used. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of convergent evolution in species that are not closely related and how selection pressures are linked to analogous structures; TWO examples of scientific evidence and how the methods can be used to determine the physical similarities are convergent evolution as opposed to divergent. Selection pressures: long flexible body for efficient swimming/thrust/movement in water and low profile from predators; lack of paired fins for burrowing and moving through tight spaces; mucus for avoiding predators/making them difficult to grasp; tolerance of low oxygen environments to access niches other organisms cannot. Scientific methods: comparative anatomy (biologists compare analogous and homologous structures); molecular biology (compare proteins/DNA/mtDNA – species that look alike but have different DNA sequences show convergent evolution); fossil record (fossils showing same trait in distantly related species indicate convergence); biogeography (analyse where species live and if traits came about independently). N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: Tetraploid treefrogs

The gray treefrog (Dryophytes versicolor) and Cope’s gray treefrog (Dryophytes chrysoscelis) are identical in physical characteristics and behaviour. However, the two species can be identified by different mating calls and chromosome numbers.

The tetraploid gray treefrog is related to the diploid Cope’s gray treefrog and is thought to have evolved through multiple hybridisation events, with different diploid ancestors. Gray treefrogs have double the number of chromosomes. This has caused their mating call to be a slower musical call than that of Cope’s gray treefrog, which is faster and more high-pitched.

The treefrogs share similar habitats, but the two species do not interbreed.

Refer to Figure 6 (Polyploid speciation in treefrogs), which shows the gray treefrog as a stable species for millions of years (tetraploid, D. versicolor 4N), with multiple hybridisation events occurring over thousands of years between diploid ancestors (4N), leading to Cope’s gray treefrog (D. chrysoscelis sp. C, 2N).

Discuss processes that caused the gray treefrog and Cope’s gray treefrog to become separate species with different evolutionary patterns. You may use diagrams to support your answer.

In your answer, include discussion of:
• hybridisation and polyploidy, including definitions
• how polyploidy can produce hybrid frogs
• why the process of speciation in treefrogs is an example of sympatric speciation and not allopatric speciation
• why this is an example of punctuated equilibrium and not gradualism.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define hybridisation and polyploidy; describe sympatric speciation, allopatric speciation,...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define hybridisation (when two different species or genetically different populations interbreed); polyploidy (when a normally diploid cell/organism gets a second set of chromosomes, occurs when there are errors in meiosis/gamete formation, chromosomes fail to separate/non-disjunction during meiosis, producing diploid 2n gametes instead of haploid n gametes). Accept a well annotated diagram. Describe sympatric speciation; allopatric speciation; punctuated equilibrium; gradualism. Merit: Explain how polyploidy produces hybrid frogs; sympatric speciation; allopatric speciation; punctuated equilibrium vs gradualism. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of how polyploidy can produce hybrid frogs and why the process of speciation in treefrogs is an example of sympatric speciation and not allopatric species; why this is an example of punctuated equilibrium and not gradualism. Hybridisation in the gray treefrog: Cope’s gray treefrog and other extinct species produced polyploid (diploid) gametes. These different species with polyploidy (2n) gametes interbred to produce hybrids that were tetraploid (4n). Therefore the offspring/hybrids were an instant species as they could not reproduce with either parent species due to differences in chromosome number. Gene flow could not occur/gametes were incompatible due to postzygotic mechanisms. The gray treefrog can reproduce only with other polyploidy individuals to form a new species (instantly). This is sympatric speciation because the frogs lived in the same geographic region and gene flow could have occurred. It is not allopatric as there is no geographic barrier separating the population. This is punctuated equilibrium because the species has developed in a short period of time/instant species in a small number of generations/one generation. In contrast gradualism is slow continuous change with small changes accumulating over millions of years; therefore this example cannot be gradualism because the hybrids could not mate with either parent species (2n) as the hybrid had double the number of chromosomes (4n). N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.
